exposure.construction: Six synthetic cases authored from the approved policy documents before evaluation; N01 and N02 differ only in the accepted progress pair and its downstream consequence.

cases.scenario: A campus-account email says the learner has five minutes to keep access by signing in through its reset link. The discussion concerns how the timer helps the sender obtain account credentials.

target.area_text: Explain how the five-minute deadline in this campus-account email can rush a learner past checks and into giving credentials to a fake sign-in page.

history.content: Think about the five-minute timer. How could that help the sender get someone's account password?

cases.learner: The timer makes me worry about losing access, so I might rush without checking where the link goes. If it leads to the sender's fake campus login, typing my password there gives the sender that password.
cases.rationale: The current learner explains the complete target mechanism in the original situation. Describing the risk is not announcing an intention to follow the link. Accepted Pending to Covered evidence completes this item without a quiz. Compare N02: the classification is identical while the trusted prior progress pair changes assessment eligibility.
cases.changed_factor: Accepted target progress pair: pending/none versus partially_covered/basic; all instructional input text is identical.

cases.scenario: A campus-account email says the learner has five minutes to keep access by signing in through its reset link. The discussion concerns how the timer helps the sender obtain account credentials.

target.area_text: Explain how the five-minute deadline in this campus-account email can rush a learner past checks and into giving credentials to a fake sign-in page.

history.content: Think about the five-minute timer. How could that help the sender get someone's account password?

cases.learner: The timer makes me worry about losing access, so I might rush without checking where the link goes. If it leads to the sender's fake campus login, typing my password there gives the sender that password.
cases.rationale: The same sufficient explanation now advances an already partial item to covered. Its final application assessment becomes due on the next eligible teacher request. The event vocabulary and evidence judgment stay the same as N01; prior accepted progress determines whether the covered item awaits assessment.
cases.changed_factor: Accepted target progress pair: pending/none versus partially_covered/basic; all instructional input text is identical.

cases.scenario: A chat account using a club treasurer's name asks for a membership payment. The learner has already noticed that the name could be copied but has not explained why that undermines the payment request's claimed identity.

target.area_text: Explain why a familiar display name on a payment-request chat does not establish that the sender is the real club treasurer.

history.content: Someone else might use the same display name.
Yes. What does that mean for deciding who actually sent this payment request?

cases.learner: I still only know that names can match. I don't understand how that tells us anything about who's asking for the money.
cases.rationale: The learner repeats the already recorded incomplete component and explicitly leaves its consequence unresolved. No new status-changing event is supported. Uncertainty is not a factual misconception, and partial evidence continues tutoring without making an assessment due.

cases.scenario: The learner is revisiting a purported music-service warning after incorrectly treating its padlock as proof of an official website. The target remains in review after that misconception.

target.area_text: Explain why an HTTPS padlock on this music-service sign-in page does not prove that the page belongs to the real service.

history.content: The padlock proves this is the real music service.
A padlock means the connection is encrypted. A scammer can also run an encrypted site. What would you change about your conclusion for this page?

cases.learner: I was treating encryption as proof of who owns the page. The padlock only protects the connection to whichever site I'm on, so even a fake music login can have one. It doesn't prove the real service runs this page.
cases.rationale: The learner repairs the misconception in the same concrete situation. Even a sufficient corrected explanation first moves a review target to partial. Tutoring continues; a later full demonstration must reach covered before a new final assessment becomes due.

cases.scenario: Earlier tutoring concerned verifying an unsolicited payroll email through a known workplace channel. Without being asked for another example, the learner now connects that principle to an in-person ticket-payment demand presented on a poster.

target.area_text: Verify an unexpected request using a trusted channel obtained independently of the request, as discussed for the payroll email.

history.content: For that payroll email, I should ask someone whether it's real.
Consider where you would get a trustworthy way to contact the payroll team.

cases.learner: That also applies to a poster I saw outside the community hall saying concert tickets must be paid for through its QR code. I'd leave the code alone and call the hall using the number in my existing booking confirmation. A fake poster could supply both a fake payment page and a fake contact number, so I need a route I already trust.
cases.rationale: The learner independently applies the verification principle with sound reasoning to a physical poster, QR payment demand, and preexisting booking contact. This materially different application directly completes the non-covered target, bypassing assessment rather than treating every Partial to Covered transition as assessment due.

cases.scenario: A suspicious conference-livestream message says a free seat disappears in two minutes. The narrow learning item concerns the pressure created by that timer. The learner separately proposes opening the suspect registration link out of curiosity.

target.area_text: Explain how the two-minute expiry claim in this livestream message pressures recipients to act before checking the offer.

history.content: The short timer makes it feel urgent.
How can that feeling change the checks someone makes before responding?

cases.learner: Thinking the seat will vanish makes people rush, so they can skip checking who runs the event and whether the offer is real. I understand that trick, but I would still click this registration link just to see what it looks like.
cases.rationale: The learner fully explains the narrow pressure mechanism without asserting that the link is safe. The separate stated unsafe click intention requires immediate protection, including its conditional wording. Target evidence can advance Partial to Covered while protection defers assessment preparation; the outstanding assessment survives that deferral while the evidence remains valid.
